articles.title: A referendum leading where?
articles.content: IT seems the regime has decided to push ahead with a referendum on the creation of new provinces, setting aside the intense controversy over the matter. The minister for parliamentary affairs had earlier declared that a referendum on the issue “will happen”; the defence minister nowsaysthe process is likely to move forward early next year. Meanwhile, Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari, the chairman of the PPP, warned that any “forced” attempt to divide provinces — particularly Sindh — could lead to bloodshed. His statement reflects an extremely volatile situation in the country’s second-largest province. It marks the widening political divide over the proposed referendum, a complex, constitutionally and politically sensitive matter involving a reset of the system, and contradicts the defence minister’s assertion that all stakeholders were close to reaching a consensus on the issue. The differences seem too wide to bridge. The PPP is a critical stakeholder in the power structure that emerged from the controversial 2024 elections. Yet for all the compromises its leadership has made — compromises that have undermined the democratic process — the party cannot afford to concede, given the strength of the political reaction the issue has provoked in its bastion of power. Seemingly under pressure, Bilawal is now even calling for “restoring the supremacy of parliament, trust in the judiciary and the electoral system”. It is an interesting development, given that his party played a critical role in getting the 26th and 27th Amendments passed — amendments that have drastically curtailed the independence of the judiciary and further diminished public trust in it. The party has also been a beneficiary of the political system created through manipulated elections. Public trust in state institutions cannot be restored until those anti-democratic amendments are reversed. The entire debate on this critical issue is taking place outside of parliament. Notwithstanding the young PPP chairman’s newfound rhetoric, parliament has long since lost its supremacy under the shadow of creeping authoritarianism. The idea of resetting the system through a referendum cannot be seen in isolation; it seems part of a move to consolidate autocracy further. Interestingly, the entire idea of a “system reset” and a referendum has been triggered byMohsin Naqvi, the interior minister whose close association with the powers that be is well known. And the entire debate on this critical issue is taking place outside of parliament. Interestingly, the controversy triggered by Naqvi’s repeated remarks about the collapse of the system and the urgency of resetting it has also prompted some cabinet ministers to question the motive behind the whole campaign. It has brought the divisions within the ruling party into the open. While the minister for parliamentary affairs and the defence minister have endorsed the reset and referendum plan, the prime minister and the PML-N leadership are conspicuous by their silence on this important constitutional matter. At the same time, there are signs that the uneasy ruling coalition is unravelling, with public polemics breaking out among the allies. Federal Minister Salik Hussain of the PML-Q isengaged in a legal battlewith the Punjab chief minister over alleged corruption charges. It is getting uglier, with other members of the group joining the fracas. The public exchange of allegations between the two federal ministers — Rana Sanaullah and Mohsin Naqvi — exposes the disarray within the cabinet. The government looks more like a rudderless ship with no one in charge. It seems the prime minister is more interested in foreign visits than in attending to domestic affairs. For him, it seems, these trips abroad earn his government the legitimacy it lacks at home. While the debate on the system reset and the referendum rages on in various public forums and in individual statements by federal ministers, the government has yet to come out with any concrete plan for an “administrative reset”, or with the question that would be framed for the vote in the referendum. No plan has been presented before the cabinet either, nor deliberated within the ruling coalition. It leaves us wondering where this plan is being prepared. Still, the defence minister insists that a joint document would be prepared with input from all stakeholders to ensure that the proposal is acceptable to everyone. “It will be a joint document in which all the stakeholders will have their input,” he said in an interview with a private TV channel. He also appears hopeful that an agreement on a joint document could be reached by the end of the year. Notwithstanding his optimism, the latest statement from Bilawal rejecting any proposal for the creation of a new administrative unit in Sindh or the holding of a referendum indicates that no discussion is taking place among the stakeholders. A major question is whether the same question will be framed for the entire country, or separate questions for each province. How can a vote in favour of creating new provinces be applied to Sindh, where an elected assembly has already rejected any such proposal? A referendum could create a political crisis that could bring down the entire edifice. It is certainly a bad idea for the unity of the country. There is a real need for decentralisation and for empowering elected local governments, and there are constitutional provisions that need to be implemented through a mandate from parliament. But the idea of creating new provinces outside the constitutional process — and that too through a referendum — could be disastrous. Intriguingly, the referendum issue has been raised at a time when the country is in the midst of political and economic instability and serious internal and external challenges. The two strategically located provinces, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, are facing violent militancy that presents an existential threat to the country. Now the reset and referendum plan has dangerously polarised Sindh. Can the country afford further political instability in the face of internal and external security challenges? There seems to be no realisation where the proposed referendum on a critical constitutional question would lead to. We also know how the referendum is manipulated to get positive results.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Cashless divide
articles.content: IMAGINE a woman in Islamabad arriving at a government office to pay a fee. She has the money, but no bank account and no smartphone of her own. The counter no longer accepts cash. The official points her towards a QR code. She asks someone nearby to make the payment for her. The payment goes through, but she has had to depend on a stranger to make it. This is a hypothetical situation, but it captures a problem beneath the government’splan to make Islamabad cashlessby the end of December. Do people have the means to participate? And what happens to those who do not? There are good reasons to encourage digital payments. They can make transactions easier to trace, reduce delays and help bring economic activity into the formal system. Raast and other payment infrastructure can make this possible at a scale that cash cannot. But encouraging digital payments is different from withdrawing cash before people have a workable alternative. That distinction matters. The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics’ Household Integrated Economic Survey 2024-25 puts the gap in perspective. Internet use among individuals stands at 57 per cent, falling to 49pc in rural areas, compared with 69pc in urban areas. Only half the population owns a mobile phone. Ownership is 69pc among men and 39pc among women. These figures do not tell us how many people can use a banking application, but they do show how uneven access to the basic tools of a cashless economy remains. People should not be turned away from a government office because they cannot make a digital payment. The gap is even wider when we look at access to financial services. According to the World Bank’s Global Findex 2025, based on 2024 data, only 12pc of women in Pakistan have an account, compared with 42pc of men. Digital payment use stands at 13pc for women and 40pc for men. Among the poorest 40pc of adults, only 9pc made digital payments, compared with 33pc among the wealthiest 60pc. For someone with a bank account, a smartphone and reliable internet, cashless payments may simply be more convenient. Someone paying in cash, living on an irregular income, sharing a phone or unfamiliar with digital interfaces may experience the same change as an additional expense. They may have to travel to an agent, pay a fee or ask someone else to make the transaction. They may also be unable to pay when a system is unavailable. The fact that everyone is being asked to use the same system does not mean everyone is equally able to use it. This becomes a more serious concern when the state makes digital payment the only option. From Dec 1, Islamabad’s ICT administration and CDA departments are expected to stop accepting cash. What will happen to someone who has no bank account or cannot use a digital application? Will there be assisted payment facilities? What happens during a network outage, a failed transfer or a disputed transaction? People should not be turned away from a government office because they cannot make a digital payment. Access is only part of the issue. A cashless economy also changes the information generated by ordinary transactions. A digital payment can create a record of who paid whom, how much and when. Depending on the system, it may also be linked to a location or other identifying information. Over time, these records can reveal patterns of work, movement, consumption and association. Of course, this does not mean government departments can simply access everyone’s financial records. That depends on the legal powers they have and the arrangements governing access to the information. But as more everyday activity moves onto digital payment systems, these questions become harder to ignore. Pakistan’s wider digital transformation makes this concern more immediate. Government departments are developing systems to exchange data, while digital identity and AI-assisted services are becoming part of policy discussions. Much of the promise of these systems lies in bringing information from different sources together. But that also creates the possibility of using information beyond the reason it was originally collected. Data generated to complete a payment should not become available for unrelated profiling or decision-making simply because it is technically possible to combine datasets. This raises some basic questions. Who can access transaction data, and for what purpose? How long is it kept? What safeguards apply when banks, payment providers and public bodies are involved? Can individuals find out if their information has been misused and seek a remedy? Pakistan has sectoral financial regulations and legal protections, but it still lacks an enacted, comprehensive personal data protection law. As the amount of financial information being generated grows, the absence of clear and enforceable rules becomes harder to justify. The government should measure Cashless Islamabad by more than the number of merchants displaying QR codes. It needs to establish who is being left out and provide assisted, low-cost ways to pay. Cash or another accessible alternative should remain available where digital access cannot reasonably be assumed, particularly for essential public services. A policy deadline cannot substitute for evidence that these arrangements actually work. There should also be clear procedures for failed transactions, refunds and complaints. Access to payment data must be limited by law and purpose, with proper audit trails and independent oversight. Moving towards digital payments may help document economic activity and make transactions easier. But before making cash unavailable, the government needs to ask a more basic question: can people actually use the alternatives being offered to them? The state is changing more than the way citizens pay. It is changing the conditions on which they participate in public and economic life. That change should make participation easier, not leave people behind because of their income, gender, location or access to technology. The writer is a technology lawyer specialising in data protection.
articles.author: Salma Khan

articles.title: Justice or just this?
articles.content: THE wheels of international justice tend to grind slowly. The Gambia launched its complaint against Myanmar at The Hague in November 2019. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered its verdict last Thursday, seven years later. Following the unprecedented finding that the state was indeed guilty of genocide against the Rohingya minority, the biggest question now is whether it will make much difference to the survivors, most of whom found refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh. Hundreds of thousands more are scattered across various other countries including India and Pakistan, but mostly concentrated in Thailand and Malaysia. The latter, which last month welcomed U Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s president and former military chief, regularly threatens deportation. The visiting leader offered to take back all citizens; however, a 1982 law stripped most Rohingya of citizenship. The community’s roots in northern Rakhine state go back centuries, yet politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have long tended to pejoratively (and inaccurately) refer to them as ‘Bengalis’. In the early stages of the ICJ case, Suu Kyi even turned up in The Hague to defend Myanmar’s hybrid regime against the charge of genocide. Suu Kyi had defended Myanmar’s regime against the genocide charge. At the time she served as the popularly elected ‘state counsellor’ in a political set-up dominated by the Tatmadaw. Within little more than a year, she was deposed in a military coup and thrown behind bars. By then she had lost much of the international respect she had built up over decades as a defender of democracy and human rights. Suu Kyi remains under detention (albeit not in jail), while red carpets are regularly rolled out for Min Aung Hlaing by his neighbours. The switch from military fatigues to civilian garb ahead of last April’s elections instantly rendered him more palatable to purported democracies in the region. Others, however, were less apprehensive from the start. Beijing, for instance, is reported to have courted the junta set up in Naypyidaw after the 2021 coup while also backing some of the insurgencies ranged against it, but pulled back its support from the latter once it became apparent that the rebels might actually thrash the Tatmadaw. Partly as a consequence, state forces have been gaining ground, although large parts of the country remain under rebel control and the civil war is far from over. Some of its components, notably the Karen state insurgents, have been at war with the state since soon after Burma, as it was then known, won independence in 1948. Even before that, some Muslim-majority areas evidently sought to become part of East Pakistan. But Mohammad Ali Jinnah demurred, and the Burmese leadership said no. Across much of Asia and Africa, history and geography are often at odds in the national boundaries bequeathed by retreating empires. However, multiethnic entities are not necessarily destined to be failed states, provided prejudice can be cast aside. As former Human Rights Watch chief Kenneth Roth puts it, “Myanmar has 135 recognised ethnic groups but refuses to accept the Rohingya as the 136th.” The state has also been in combat for decades with other ethnic groups, but ‘clearance operations’ with a view to some manner of extermination were reserved for Rakhine. After seven years of litigation, the ICJ has given Myanmar another two years to respond to its rulings on restitution, reunification and/or compensation. What can anyone expect in the meanwhile from the UN Security Council, or the individual states that have lately re-embraced Myanmar despite its continuing excesses against its own population? The ICJ verdict has been greeted as an indication of its eventual ruling in South Africa’s case against Israel. It’s true that the criteria invoked in accepting the charges against Myanmar — making clear that ‘counter-insurgency’, ‘counterterrorism’ or ethnic cleansing efforts are not incompatible with genocidal intent — suggest that the case against Israel is a slam dunk. There is no dearth of official statements dehumanising Palestinians and vowing extermination. Horrendous as they are, the number of child deaths cited in the verdict on Myanmar is but a fraction of the toll that Israel has notched up. And I hope South Africa will add the documentary NAZA to its brief. Six of the ICJ’s 15 judges dissented from the majority verdict. The pattern of voting might be different in the case of Israel. But no decision is expected before 2030-31 at the earliest. By then, even if Israel is convicted for a genocide it continues to commit, will it make any difference? Or will it be just another feather in the cap of a postwar legal order that has always struggled to stay relevant in the face of superpower-sized odds? Now, and possibly in the future, one could ask the ICJ: thank you for your verdict, but where’s the justice?
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: Raising our sons
articles.content: IN June, a seven-year-old girl in Sargodha went to a grocery store and never returned. In August, an 18-month-old in Karachi lost her life after being sexually assaulted by a teenage relative. Two weeks later, Hina Javed, a 45-year-old professional, was foundraped and murderedin her own home in Rawalpindi. Days later, a five-year-old girl in Haripur who had gone out to play wasfound deadin a well. These cases broke through in a single summer; many more never did. Each time, Pakistan said “never again,” then turned the page. On paper, Pakistan has made progress.The Anti-Rape Act of 2021and the rules that followed strengthened how rape is investigated and tried, and how survivors are protected. Yet law ministry figures, reported byDawn, record 47,452 cases across five categories of rape-related offences in the four provinces between 2021 and mid-2026. And that is only the reported picture: the Senate Functional Committee on Human Rights noted that an estimated 70 per cent of gender-based violence incidents go unreported. In Pakistan, rape is treated as a woman’s problem. After every case, we ask the same questions. Where were her parents? Why was she alone? Why did she let him in? The questions are always about her. But we rarely ask the questions that matter. Who are these men and boys? Where did they learn this? And who around them noticed something and said nothing? In Pakistan, rape is treated as a woman’s problem even though it is something men do, most often men she knows. In cases of reported child sexual abuse, child protection group Sahil found that acquaintances remained the most common category of abusers in 2025. We have spent decades teaching our daughters to be careful but barely begun teaching our sons. Nothing excuses these crimes. But we must look honestly at how boys grow up. Many learn early that anger is the only feeling a man shows, and that a sister’s freedom is his to police. Few ever learn about consent, at home or in school. When they struggle, there is rarely anyone to talk to, because mental health is still a whisper in most homes. By official count, nearly 12 million boys are out of school. Many grow up without the guidance, support and opportunities that help shape their understanding of relationships and respect. Poverty does not make a rapist, and rape happens in wealthy homes too. But do we want to leave a generation to learn about women from the street and the screen? In the classroom. Every child should learn what safe and unsafe touch is, what consent means, and that respect for women is not optional. This belongs in the school curriculum, not in a one-day workshop. Through UNDP’s work, from strengthening gender-responsive justice and the security sector to supporting Pakistan’s first national strategy on technology-facilitated gender-based violence and expanding women’s economic opportunities, I have seen why institutional reform matters. But I also believe that institutions are too often asked to correct attitudes that have hardened long before a man enters a police station, courtroom or workplace. Which is why men must own this work. For fathers, it starts with how they speak to women at home and with the first time they teach a son that consent is not negotiable. Men who run governments, police stations, courtrooms, mosques and newsrooms can stop interrogating what she was wearing and start asking what he did. Every man who laughs at the joke, forwards the video or keeps the secret is making a choice. Young men, online and in the street, can challenge their peers in ways no elder can. Most of all, we need to talk about this far more consistently and loudly. Advocacy campaigns come in short bursts: around international days or after a case trends, before falling silent until another assault dominates the airwaves. When I was growing up in Vietnam, the government ran a family planning campaign with one simple message: “boy or girl, two children are enough.” It was on billboards, on television and on the radio, year after year, until it became common sense. The context was different, but the lesson stayed with me. A message repeated often enough, for long enough, can reshape what a society considers normal. Pakistan can do the same. Government, media and advertisers could carry one national message, every day, not once a year: rape is a man’s choice and a man’s shame, and every man has a responsibility to speak up. Every man and boy in this summer’s headlines was shaped in Pakistani homes, schools, and communities, by what the men around them said, did, and allowed. That is where this begins, and where it must end. Pakistan does not only need to protect its daughters. It must raise its sons better. The writer is deputy resident representative, UNDP Pakistan.
articles.author: Van Nguyen

articles.title: Whose life next?
articles.content: THEkillingof television anchor Rabia Ahsan in Rawalpindi this month revives a question Pakistan has yet to answer: how can we better protect women from those who threaten them? In August, digital media executive Hina Javedwas found murdered. Last year, thekilling of teenager Sana Yousafin Islamabad and the shooting of a couple in Balochistan for choosing each other provoked public outrage. Though circumstances differ, the deaths show women may pay with their lives for asserting their independence or defying the expectations of others. As the world observes the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women today, Pakistan must also remember those whose suffering never makes headlines. According to the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, at least 470 women were killed in the name of so-called honour in 2025. Rights group Sahil recorded 3,172 cases of gender-based violence in the first half of 2026. These figures do not capture the abuse hidden by fear, financial dependence and pressure to protect family reputations. For many women, violence is not a lone incident but a prolonged pattern of intimidation, control and isolation, endured behind closed doors with little outside help. Each high-profile killing brings grief, condemnation and demands for justice. But outrage fades while the failures that allow violence to flourish remain. Hina Javed’s case illustrates this: nearly three months after her death, her trial has yet to begin, though police have submitted the investigation report. For women facing threats from husbands, relatives or rejected suitors, delays send a frightening message. Many hesitate to seek help, fearing that complaints will be dismissed as family disputes or that reporting abuse will provoke further retaliation. This year’s UN campaign calls for justice, protection for survivors and an end to impunity — goals that will remain elusive in Pakistan unless laws against violence are effectively enforced. Complaints must be taken seriously; repeated threats and stalking must trigger prompt police intervention; and investigations must proceed without political or family pressure. Officers must be trained to recognise escalating danger, particularly where earlier assaults, death threats or access to weapons are involved, and to connect women at risk with emergency protection rather than send them home. Women need accessible shelters, legal aid and financial support that make leaving an abusive situation a realistic option. Schools, families and community leaders must challenge the notion that women’s choices can sully someone’s ‘honour’. The test for Pakistan lies not in how loudly it mourns a murdered woman, but whether it acts to protect the next one while she is still alive.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Oman oil deal
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S new oil supply agreement with Oman comes at a difficult time for its energy sector. Under the agreement, Oman will supply petroleum products and extend a $200m credit facility. The credit line is important because Pakistan’s fuel imports place considerable pressure on its forex reserves. Deferred payments can ease immediate dollar requirements and provide greater flexibility in financing its purchases. Similar arrangements with other suppliers have helped manage import obligations. But credit facilities are borrowing arrangements at the end of the day. The agreement’s significance, however, extends beyond the deferred payment facility. The arrangement would offer some relief amid uncertainty over regional oil supplies. The continuing disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has exposed Pakistan’s vulnerability to regional conflicts. The country imports nearly 80-85pc of its petroleum requirements, with much of its supplies traditionally passing through this critical maritime passage. Oman offers an important alternative because its ports provide access to the Arabian Sea outside Hormuz. This geographical advantage could help Pakistan reduce its exposure to disruptions affecting traditional Gulf supply routes. The state must ensure that the agreement translates into reliable supplies at competitive prices. More importantly, the arrangement should prompt a wider rethink of the nation’s energy security. The country has repeatedly faced difficulties whenever international conflicts disrupt oil and gas supplies. Its over-dependence on imported petroleum leaves the economy exposed to external shocks, drains foreign exchange and adds to domestic inflation. Building strategic petroleum reserves, improving storage capacity and developing alternative supply routes must receive greater attention. At the same time, Islamabad also needs to reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels through faster adoption of indigenous renewable energy. Solar and wind power can lower the country’s exposure to international fuel markets over time. The agreement with Oman is welcome. But a new supplier and a credit line cannot, by themselves, resolve Pakistan’s energy vulnerabilities. Energy security requires a sustained reduction in import dependence.
articles.author: Editorial
